# Read in spousal data

This script will read in Census and ACS data from 1960 to 2019 to construct broad interracial marriage patterns over that entire time period. The extract downloaded from IPUMS includes only individuals with the marital status of "married, spouse present." I also restrict the sample to men and then attach information about various partner characteristics via IPUMS extraction system. 

```{r}
#| label: read-spousal-data

census <- read_fwf(here("data", "data_raw", "acs_census", "usa_00149.dat.gz"),
                   col_positions = fwf_cols(YEAR = c(1,4),
                                            SAMPLE = c(5, 10),
                                            HHWT = c(32, 41),
                                            PERWT = c(76, 85),
                                            PERWT_SP = c(128, 137),
                                            STRATA = c(59, 70),
                                            CLUSTER = c(42, 54),
                                            REGION = c(55, 56),
                                            STATEFIP = c(57, 58),
                                            SEX = 86,
                                            AGE = c(87, 89),
                                            MARRNO = 91,
                                            YRMARR = c(92, 95),
                                            AGEMARR = c(96, 97),
                                            RACED = c(99, 101),
                                            RACHSING = 119,
                                            HISPAN = 102,
                                            BPL = c(106, 108),
                                            YRIMMIG = c(114, 117),
                                            EDUCD = c(122, 124),
                                            SEX_SP = 138,
                                            AGE_SP = c(139, 141),
                                            MARRNO_SP = 142,
                                            AGEMARR_SP = c(147, 148),
                                            RACED_SP = c(149, 151),
                                            RACHSING_SP = 161,
                                            HISPAN_SP = 152,
                                            BPL_SP = c(153, 155),
                                            YRIMMIG_SP = c(156, 159),
                                            EDUCD_SP = c(164, 166),
                                            QRACE = 126,
                                            QHISPAN = 125,
                                            QRACE_SP = 168,
                                            QHISPAN_SP = 167),
                   col_types = cols(.default = "i", STRATA = "c", CLUSTER = "c",
                                    HHWT = "d", PERWT = "d", PERWT = "d"))
```

In more recent data we will have some same sex couples. To keep consistency across the time I will focus on heterosexual couples. The full data contain some male-male couples in the sample, so these need to be removed.

```{r}
#| label: check-spouse-sex

table(census$SEX, census$SEX_SP)

census <- census |>
  filter(SEX_SP == 2)

table(census$SEX, census$SEX_SP)
```


# Read in cohabitor data

```{r}
#| label: read-spousal-data

cohab <- read_fwf(here("data", "data_raw", "acs_census", "usa_00150.dat.gz"),
                  col_positions = fwf_cols(YEAR = c(1,4),
                                           SAMPLE = c(5, 10),
                                           SERIAL = c(11, 18),
                                           HHWT = c(32, 41),
                                           PERWT = c(76, 85),
                                           STRATA = c(59, 70),
                                           CLUSTER = c(42, 54),
                                           REGION = c(55, 56),
                                           STATEFIP = c(57, 58),
                                           RELATED = c(88, 91),
                                           SEX = 92,
                                           AGE = c(93, 95),
                                           RACED = c(98, 100),
                                           RACHSING = 117,
                                           HISPAN = 101,
                                           BPL = c(105, 107),
                                           YRIMMIG = c(113, 116),
                                           EDUCD = c(120, 122),
                                           QRACE = 124,
                                           QHISPAN = 123),
                  col_types = cols(.default = "i", STRATA = "c", CLUSTER = "c",
                                   HHWT = "d", PERWT = "d", PERWT = "d"))
```

Now combine heads of households with unmarried partners to get cohabitations and add this to the full data.

```{r}
#| label: add-cohabitors

# get unique household ids
cohab <- cohab |>
  mutate(hhid = paste0(SAMPLE, SERIAL))


hh_cohab <- cohab |> filter(RELATED == 101)
partner_cohab <- cohab |> filter(RELATED == 1114) |>
  rename(PERWT_SP = PERWT,
         SEX_SP = SEX,
         AGE_SP = AGE,
         RACED_SP = RACED,
         RACHSING_SP = RACHSING,
         HISPAN_SP = HISPAN,
         BPL_SP = BPL,
         YRIMMIG_SP = YRIMMIG,
         EDUCD_SP = EDUCD,
         QRACE_SP = QRACE,
         QHISPAN_SP = QHISPAN) |>
  select(hhid, ends_with("_SP"))

# join them back up - right join to drop other kinds of heads of household
cohab <- hh_cohab |>
  right_join(partner_cohab, by = "hhid") |>
  # only opposite sex cohabitors
  filter(SEX != SEX_SP) |>
  select(-SERIAL, -RELATED, -hhid) |>
  mutate(union_type = "cohabitation")

# now add to full data
census <- census |>
  mutate(union_type = "marriage") |>
  bind_rows(cohab)

# check
table(census$YEAR, census$union_type)

# free up memory
rm(cohab, hh_cohab, partner_cohab)
gc()
```


# Remove race allocated cases

Lets remove any cases that were allocated race or hispanicity for either spouse, as spousal race may have been used in the allocation procedure. A zero value indicates an unedited response on the quality flags, although in years where the quality flag is not available we get missing values that need to be checked.

```{r}
table(census$YEAR, census$QRACE, exclude = NULL)
table(census$YEAR, census$QHISPAN_SP, exclude = NULL)

census <- census |>
  filter((is.na(QRACE) | QRACE == 0),
         (is.na(QRACE_SP) | QRACE_SP == 0),
         (is.na(QHISPAN) | QHISPAN == 0),
         (is.na(QHISPAN_SP) | QHISPAN_SP == 0))

summary(census$QRACE)
summary(census$QRACE_SP)
summary(census$QHISPAN)
summary(census$QHISPAN_SP)
```

# Code variables

States are entered as numeric FIPS codes. I will use the `tidycensus` package to merge in the `fips_codes` data to get state abbreviations.

```{r}
#| label: code-state-fips

census <- fips_codes |> 
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(STATEFIP = as.numeric(state_code)) |>
  select(state, STATEFIP) |>
  distinct() |>
  right_join(census, by = "STATEFIP")
```

## Coding race

Ok, now I am ready to code most of the variables we care about. The primary variable of concern is the race variable. Because I am doing this over a large time period I are limited in how I caan code race consistently. I also want to keep the categories small so that I will have a large enough sample size for each group in each year. For the main analysis, I will use the following categories:

- White
- Black
- Indigenous (American Indian/Alaska Native and Pacific Islander)
- Asian
- Hispanic

Reliable data on Hispanic identification is not available until 1980. IPUMS does provide a Hispanic identifier for earlier years that is primarily based on surnames, but this cannot be used by for interracial marriage because the identifier is the same for spouses. The 1970 data do contain responses to the first Hispanicity question on Form 1, but these responses have been shown to be inconsistent with later responses from 1980 on. I did test this response, and found a substantial decrease in Hispanic intermarriage from 1970 to 1980 that is inconsistent with general trends.

The 1980 data included a race category 650 which was for "Other Asian/Pacific Islander groups." This category was in keeping with the Census decision to collapse the Asian and Pacific Islander category together in most 1980 and 1990 reported statistics. For a variety of historical reasons (e.g. discourses of miscegenation) I think it makes much more sense to treat Pacific Islanders as an indigenous populations. However, to do so I need to deal with the 650 cases in 1980. I do this by imputation discussed below further.

I also include five biracial groups from 2000 on that have a large enough sample to analyze:

- White-Black
- White-Indigenous
- White-Asian
- Black-Indigenous
- Black-Asian

```{r}
#| label: code-race

# we code race in the most detailed categories first
code_race <- function(raced, hispan, year) {
  
  subrace <- case_when(
    hispan != 0 & raced == 100 & year > 1970 ~ "WhiteHispanic",
    hispan != 0 & raced == 200 & year > 1970 ~ "BlackHispanic",
    hispan != 0 & raced == 700 & year > 1970 ~ "OtherHispanic",
    hispan != 0 & year > 1970 ~ "ResidualHispanic",
    raced == 100 ~ "White",
    raced == 200 ~ "Black",
    (raced >= 300 & raced <= 399) ~ "AIAN",
    raced == 630 | (raced >= 680 & raced <= 699) ~ "PI",
    # leaving out 650 Other Asian or API in 1980 only
    (raced >= 400 & raced <= 500) | raced %in% c(620, 642, 668) ~ "EastAsian",
    raced %in% c(600, 640, 660:663, 665:667) ~ "SEAsian",
    raced %in% c(610, 641, 643, 664, 669:670) ~ "SouthAsian",
    raced %in% c(671:679) ~ "OtherAsian",
    # lets do major biracial groups
    raced == 801 ~ "White-Black",
    raced == 802 ~ "White-AIAN",
    (raced >= 820 & raced <= 825) ~ "White-PI",
    raced >= 810 & raced <= 819 ~ "White-Asian",
    raced == 830 ~ "Black-AIAN",
    (raced >= 840 & raced <= 842) ~ "Black-PI",
    raced >= 831 & raced <= 838 ~ "Black-Asian")
  
  factor(subrace, 
         levels = c("White", "Black", 
                    "AIAN", "PI", 
                    "EastAsian", "SEAsian", "SouthAsian", "OtherAsian",
                    "WhiteHispanic", "BlackHispanic", "OtherHispanic", 
                    "ResidualHispanic",
                    "White-Black", "White-AIAN", "White-PI", "White-Asian", 
                    "Black-AIAN", "Black-PI", "Black-Asian"))
}

# also code best single race
code_best_race <- function(race) {
  
  best_race <- factor(race,
                      levels = 1:5,
                      labels = c("White", "Black", "AIAN", "API", "Hispanic"))
  
}

census <- census |>
  mutate(race_husband = code_race(RACED, HISPAN, YEAR),
         race_wife = code_race(RACED_SP, HISPAN_SP, YEAR),
         race_best_husband = code_best_race(RACHSING),
         race_best_wife = code_best_race(RACHSING_SP))
```

## Code additional variables

To help smooth out smaller sample sizes I group the ACS data after 2000 into three year groups of 2001-2003, 2004-2006, 2007-2009, 2010-2012, 2013-2015, and 2016-2018. They are all identified by the midpoint year. 

ACS data from 2008 onward included the year of the most recent marriage for married individuals. I can use this to determine the duration of the current marriage. The 1960, 1970, and 1980 also include a variable on married individuals age at *first* marriage. I use these to calculate duration of the current marriage, but for the earlier data period, I will only have valid duration of marriage for first marriages. 

```{r}
#| label: create-vars

# create some functions for coding data where we need to do it for both spouses
code_educ <- function(educd) {
  education <- case_when(
    educd < 62 ~ "LHS",
    educd < 70 ~ "HS",
    educd < 101 ~ "SC",
    TRUE ~ "C"
  )
  
  education <- factor(education,
                      levels = c("LHS", "HS", "SC", "C"))
  
  return(education)
}

code_generation <- function(bpl) {
  factor(if_else(bpl <= 99, "2nd+", "1st"))
}

# for the age weighting, we will need five year age groups. Just code
# by the midpoint so we can calculate means
create_age_group <- function(age) {
  
  # rather than categorical, we will use midpoints. For the open ended 
  # categories we will just go 5 above and 2 below.
  age_group <- case_when(
    age < 20 ~ 18,    # less than 20
    age < 25 ~ 22.5,  # 20-24
    age < 30 ~ 27.5,  # 25-29
    age < 35 ~ 32.5,  # 30-34
    age < 45 ~ 40,    # 35-44
    age < 55 ~ 50,    # 45-54
    age >= 55 ~ 57.5, # 55+
    TRUE ~ NA
  )
  
  return(age_group)
  
}

census <- census |>
  mutate(educ_husband = code_educ(EDUCD),
         educ_wife = code_educ(EDUCD_SP),
         age_husband = AGE,
         age_wife = AGE_SP,
         age_group_husband = create_age_group(age_husband),
         age_group_wife = create_age_group(age_wife),
         gen_husband = code_generation(BPL),
         gen_wife = code_generation(BPL_SP),
         dur_mar = case_when(
           YEAR >= 2008 ~ YEAR-YRMARR,
           YEAR <= 1980 & MARRNO == 1 ~ AGE-AGEMARR,
           YEAR <= 1980 & MARRNO_SP == 1 ~ AGE_SP-AGEMARR_SP,
           TRUE ~ NA
         ),
         region = case_when(
           REGION %in% c(11, 12) ~ "NE",
           REGION %in% c(21, 22) ~ "MW",
           REGION %in% c(31, 32, 33) ~ "S",
           REGION %in% c(41, 42) ~ "W"
         ),
         division = case_when(
           REGION == 11 ~ "New England",
           REGION == 12 ~ "Middle Atlantic",
           REGION == 21 ~ "East North Central",
           REGION == 22 ~ "West North Central",
           REGION == 31 ~ "South Atlantic",
           REGION == 32 ~ "East South Central",
           REGION == 33 ~ "West South Central",
           REGION == 41 ~ "Mountain",
           REGION == 42 ~ "Pacific"
         ),
         year = case_when(
           YEAR <= 2000 ~ YEAR,
           YEAR <= 2003 ~ 2002,
           YEAR <= 2006 ~ 2005,
           YEAR <= 2009 ~ 2008,
           YEAR <= 2012 ~ 2011,
           YEAR <= 2015 ~ 2014,
           YEAR <= 2018 ~ 2017
         )) |>
  # remove 2019
  filter(YEAR != 2019)
```

## Code weights

I don't have a couple-based weight in the data so my choice is to use the household weight or some combination of the person weights. If there was only one couple per household, then the household weight would be ideal, but that is not always the case. 

Lets look at the correlations between the weights:


```{r}
#| label: corr-weights

cor(census[,c("PERWT", "PERWT_SP", "HHWT")])
```

They are pretty tightly correlated. I think the most principled approach is to take the average of the person weights. These weights should be divided by the mean for each year.

```{r}
#| label: construct-weights

census <- census |>
  mutate(weight_sample = (PERWT + PERWT_SP) / 2)

# check on the correlation matrix
cor(census[,c("weight_sample", "PERWT", "PERWT_SP", "HHWT")])

# now normalize the weights to mean to one in each year
weight_means <- census |>
  group_by(YEAR) |>
  summarize(mean_sweight = mean(weight_sample), .groups = "drop")

census <- census |>
  left_join(weight_means, by = "YEAR") |>
  mutate(weight_sample = weight_sample / mean_sweight)

# check to make sure it means to one in each year
census |>
  group_by(YEAR) |>
  summarize(mean(weight_sample), .groups = "drop")
```

## Impute race for 650 case

Now lets impute values for the 650 (Other Asian/Pacific Islander) cases from 1980. I will use valid 1990 observations for Asian and Pacific Islander respondents for the imputation procedure. I use 1990 rather than valid 1980 responses because it has a fuller range of possible categories for Asian and Pacific Islander respondents, specifically those that would have gone into the "Other Asian/PI" 650 category in 1980. I impute via predictive mean matching using the following covariates:

- race of other partner
- age of both partners
- education of both partners
- duration of marriage
- state of residence

```{r}
#| label: impute-other-api

# first husbands
idxh <- which(census$RACED == 650 & census$HISPAN == 0)
length(idxh)
data_imph <- census |>
  filter((RACED >= 400 & RACED < 700 & HISPAN == 0) & year == "1990",
         !is.na(race_husband)) |>
  bind_rows(census[idxh,]) |>
  select(state, race_husband, race_wife, age_husband, age_wife, 
         educ_husband, educ_wife, dur_mar, year)

imph_race <- mice(data_imph, 1, defaultMethod = c("pmm", "pmm", "pmm", "polr"),
                     printFlag = FALSE) |>
  complete(1) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  filter(year == "1980") |>
  pull(race_husband)

table(imph_race)

# then wives
idxw <- which(census$RACED_SP == 650 & census$HISPAN_SP == 0)
length(idxw)
data_impw <- census |>
  filter((RACED_SP >= 400 & RACED_SP < 700 & HISPAN_SP == 0) & year == "1990",
         !is.na(race_wife)) |>
  bind_rows(census[idxw,]) |>
  select(state, race_husband, race_wife, age_husband, age_wife, 
         educ_husband, educ_wife, dur_mar, year)

impw_race <- mice(data_impw, 1, defaultMethod = c("pmm", "pmm", "pmm", "polr"),
                     printFlag = FALSE) |>
  complete(1) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  filter(year == "1980") |>
  pull(race_wife)

table(impw_race)

# now replace NA with imputed values
census[idxh, "race_husband"] <- imph_race
census[idxw, "race_wife"] <- impw_race
```

## Check yourself before you wreck yourself

Lets run some checks on our codes.

```{r}
#| label: data-coding-checks

table(census$YEAR, census$year)
table(census$EDUCD, census$educ_husband)
table(census$EDUCD_SP, census$educ_wife)
table(census$educ_husband, census$educ_wife)

table(census$race_husband)
table(census$race_wife)

table(census$RACED, census$race_husband)
table(census$RACED_SP, census$race_wife)

census |>
  group_by(YEAR) |>
  summarize(mean_dur_mar = mean(dur_mar, na.rm = TRUE),
            min_dur_mar = min(dur_mar, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  gt()
```

# Calculate joint age distributions

I want to calculate age weights that weight each couple by the joint age distribution to mimic an age distribution similar to recently married couples. To do this, I first need to calculate the joint age distribution of recent marriages in each time period. For the data from 2008 onward I can do this from the ACS data itself, by selecting partners married a year or less.

I also need this joint age distribution to be grouped into larger age groups than single years for two reasons. First, grouping will make for smoother interpolations in cases where I need to interpolate the joint distribution. Second, I will be using vital statistics report published tables to determine the joint distribution in earlier years and these tables have already grouped partners into larger age goups. The age groups that I will use in order to be able to use all tables are:

* Under 20
* 20-24
* 25-29
* 30-34
* 35-44
* 45-54
* 55 and over

Thes age groups are already coded in as numeric values in the `age_group_` variables for each spouse. I use a numeric value so that I can easily calculate means across years as a diagnostic check.

```{r}
#| label: calculate-joint-age-distribution

# long format table of joint distribution of spouse's age by year
prop_age_year_recent <- census |>
  filter(dur_mar <= 1 & YEAR >= 2008 & union_type == "marriage") |>
  group_by(age_group_husband, age_group_wife, YEAR) |>
  summarize(n_dur = n()) |>
  ungroup()

prop_age_year_recent <- census |>
  filter(dur_mar <= 1 & YEAR >= 2008 & union_type == "marriage") |>
  group_by(YEAR) |>
  summarize(n_total = n()) |>
  ungroup() |>
  right_join(prop_age_year_recent) |>
  mutate(prop = n_dur / n_total) |>
  select(age_group_husband, age_group_wife, YEAR, prop)
  
# check sums to 1 in each year
prop_age_year_recent |>
  group_by(YEAR) |>
  summarize(sum(prop)) |>
  gt()
```

The resulting joint distribution proportions are correctly summing to one in each year.

For the years 1960, 1970, 1980, and 1988, I use published tables from vital statistics reports that give the joint distribution in each year. I transcribed these tables to a google sheet avaiable [here](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1YVMMhwrIsyux6FQCPqyCqN45BLOruxLfsk60XBra1z4/edit?usp=sharing).

To prepare for reading this in, I deauthorize the `googlesheets4` package so I can read it in without having to enter authorization and I create a function that will help me convert the tables to the format I want.

```{r}
#| label: prep-read-gsheet-tables

gs4_deauth()

convert_age_string <- function(x) {
  
 x <- x |> str_remove("^wife_|^husband_")
 x <- ifelse(str_detect(x, "under_18"), "17", x)
 x <- ifelse(str_detect(x, "under_20"), "18", x)
 x <- ifelse(str_detect(x, "65_over"), "65", x)
 x <- ifelse(str_detect(x, "55_over"), "55", x)
 x <- x |>str_split_i("_", 1)
 
 x <- as.numeric(x)
 create_age_group(x)
    
}
```

## Read 1960 vital stats data

This one is a bit of a mess. Its split up by single, widowed, and divorced wives, but the age groups for widowed and divorced start with under 35 and under 25, respectively. To extend these groups across all the categories, I distribute the under 35 and under 25 cases across the full cells using the proportions found in the single wives table.

```{r}
#| label: read-1960-vsus

vsus1960_single <- read_sheet("1YVMMhwrIsyux6FQCPqyCqN45BLOruxLfsk60XBra1z4",
                              sheet = "Table 2-18 Single Bride 1960 VSUS") |>
  filter(wife_age != "wife_total") |>
  select(!husband_total) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("husband_"),
               names_to = "husband_age", values_to = "freq")

vsus1960_widowed <- read_sheet("1YVMMhwrIsyux6FQCPqyCqN45BLOruxLfsk60XBra1z4",
                              sheet = "Table 2-18 Widowed Bride 1960 VSUS") |>
  filter(wife_age != "wife_total") |>
  select(!husband_total) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("husband_"),
               names_to = "husband_age", values_to = "freq")

vsus1960_divorced <- read_sheet("1YVMMhwrIsyux6FQCPqyCqN45BLOruxLfsk60XBra1z4",
                              sheet = "Table 2-18 Divorced Bride 1960 VSUS") |>
  filter(wife_age != "wife_total") |>
  select(!husband_total) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("husband_"),
               names_to = "husband_age", values_to = "freq")

# ok first lets distribute the widowed cases
wife_ages <- c("wife_under_20", "wife_20_24", "wife_25_29", "wife_30_34")
for(husb_age in unique(vsus1960_single$husband_age)) {
  x <- vsus1960_single |> 
    filter(husband_age == husb_age & wife_age %in% wife_ages) |>
    pull(freq)
  p <- x/sum(x)
  freq <- vsus1960_widowed |>
    filter(husband_age == husb_age & wife_age == "wife_under_35") |>
    pull(freq)
  freq <- freq*p
  vsus1960_widowed <- vsus1960_widowed |>
    bind_rows(tibble(wife_age = wife_ages, husband_age = husb_age, freq = freq))
}
# now remove the under_35 cases
vsus1960_widowed <- vsus1960_widowed |>
  filter(wife_age != "wife_under_35")

# now divorced
wife_ages <- c("wife_under_20", "wife_20_24")
for(husb_age in unique(vsus1960_single$husband_age)) {
  x <- vsus1960_single |> 
    filter(husband_age == husb_age & wife_age %in% wife_ages) |>
    pull(freq)
  p <- x/sum(x)
  freq <- vsus1960_divorced |>
    filter(husband_age == husb_age & wife_age == "wife_under_25") |>
    pull(freq)
  freq <- freq*p
  vsus1960_divorced <- vsus1960_divorced |>
    bind_rows(tibble(wife_age = wife_ages, husband_age = husb_age, freq = freq))
}
# now remove the under_35 cases
vsus1960_divorced <- vsus1960_divorced |>
  filter(wife_age != "wife_under_25")

# now combine them together and continue processing
vsus1960 <- vsus1960_single |>
  bind_rows(vsus1960_widowed) |>
  bind_rows(vsus1960_divorced) |>
  mutate(age_group_husband = convert_age_string(husband_age),
         age_group_wife = convert_age_string(wife_age)) |>
  group_by(age_group_husband, age_group_wife) |>
  summarize(freq = sum(freq)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(prop = freq / sum(freq), YEAR = 1960) |>
  select(age_group_husband, age_group_wife, YEAR, prop)

# add to full joint distribution data
prop_age_year_recent <- prop_age_year_recent |>
  bind_rows(vsus1960)
```

## Read 1970 vital stats data

The 1970 data is a straightforward single table.

```{r}
#| label: read-1970-vsus

vsus1970 <- read_sheet("1YVMMhwrIsyux6FQCPqyCqN45BLOruxLfsk60XBra1z4",
                       sheet = "Table 1-28 1970 VSUS") |>
  filter(wife_age != "wife_total") |>
  select(!husband_total) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("husband_"),
               names_to = "husband_age", values_to = "freq") |>
  mutate(age_group_husband = convert_age_string(husband_age),
         age_group_wife = convert_age_string(wife_age),
         prop = freq / sum(freq)) |>
  group_by(age_group_husband, age_group_wife) |>
  summarize(prop = sum(prop)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(YEAR = 1970) |>
  select(age_group_husband, age_group_wife, YEAR, prop)

# add to full joint distribution data
prop_age_year_recent <- prop_age_year_recent |>
  bind_rows(vsus1970)
```

## Read 1980 vital stats data

The 1980 data is a straightforward single table.

```{r}
  filter(wife_age != "wife_total") |>

  summarize(prop = sum(prop)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(YEAR = 1980) |>
  select(age_group_husband, age_group_wife, YEAR, prop)

# remove existing 1980 data and replace with this one
prop_age_year_recent <- prop_age_year_recent |>
  filter(YEAR != 1980) |>
  bind_rows(vsus1980)
```

## Read 1988 vital stats data

1988 was the last year in which official vital statistics for marriage were published that I can use. This data is closer to the 1990 and 2000 data and so is a better jumping off point for the interpolations that will follow even though I won't use the 1988 proportions directly.

The 1988 data were split by race (White, Black, and Other). Interestingly, interracial couples were ignored. Combining the results together should get me a pretty good approximation of the joint distribution of the age of spouses.

```{r}
#| label: read-1988-vsus

vsus1988 <- read_sheet("1YVMMhwrIsyux6FQCPqyCqN45BLOruxLfsk60XBra1z4",
                             sheet = "Table 1-20, White Spouses, 1988 VSUS") |>
  filter(wife_age != "wife_total") |>
  select(!husband_total) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("husband_"),
               names_to = "husband_age", values_to = "freq")

vsus1988 <- read_sheet("1YVMMhwrIsyux6FQCPqyCqN45BLOruxLfsk60XBra1z4",
                             sheet = "Table 1-20, Black Spouses, 1988 VSUS") |>
  filter(wife_age != "wife_total") |>
  select(!husband_total) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("husband_"),
               names_to = "husband_age", values_to = "freq") |>
  bind_rows(vsus1988)

vsus1988 <- read_sheet("1YVMMhwrIsyux6FQCPqyCqN45BLOruxLfsk60XBra1z4",
                             sheet = "Table 1-20, Other Spouses, 1988 VSUS") |>
  filter(wife_age != "wife_total") |>
  select(!husband_total) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("husband_"),
               names_to = "husband_age", values_to = "freq") |>
  bind_rows(vsus1988)

vsus1988 <- read_sheet("1YVMMhwrIsyux6FQCPqyCqN45BLOruxLfsk60XBra1z4",
                             sheet = "Table 1-20, Spouses not stated, 1988 VSUS") |>
  filter(wife_age != "wife_total") |>
  select(!husband_total) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("husband_"),
               names_to = "husband_age", values_to = "freq") |>
  bind_rows(vsus1988)

vsus1988 <- vsus1988 |>
  mutate(age_group_husband = convert_age_string(husband_age),
         age_group_wife = convert_age_string(wife_age)) |>
  group_by(age_group_husband, age_group_wife) |>
  summarize(freq = sum(freq)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(prop = freq / sum(freq),

# add 1988 data to full age prop data
prop_age_year_recent <- prop_age_year_recent |>
  bind_rows(vsus1988)
```

## Interpolating joint distributions

I have no information on the duration of marriages between 1980 and 2008 and we have no vital statistics reports. Therefore to get joint distributions for 1990 and 2000-2007, I will need to interpolate. After experimenting with more advanced techniques, I found that a simpler linear interpolation actually provided the best fit. I first create a function to interpolate.

```{r}
#| label: function-interpolation

# create function to interpolate
interpolate_age_dist <- function(year_interp, year_start, year_end) {

  # starting and end distributions
  dist_start <- prop_age_year_recent |> 
    filter(YEAR == year_start) |>
    pull(prop)
  
  dist_end <- prop_age_year_recent |> 
    filter(YEAR == year_end) |>
    pull(prop)
  
  # simple linear interpolation outperforms more complex methods
  alpha <- (year_interp - year_start) / (year_end - year_start)  

  # Interpolate linearly between the distributions
  dist_interp <- (1 - alpha) * dist_start + alpha * dist_end
  
  # put into same format as prop_age_year_recent
  prop_age_year_recent |>
    filter(YEAR == year_end) |>
    select(age_group_husband, age_group_wife) |>
    mutate(YEAR = year_interp,
           prop = dist_interp)
}
```

Now I can do the interpolation for the missing years and add them to the full joint distribution data.

```{r}
#| label: age-interpolation

# ok lets now interpolate all needed years by what we have
years_interp <- c(1990, 2000:2007)
prop_age_year_recent <- map(years_interp, interpolate_age_dist, 1988, 2008) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  bind_rows(prop_age_year_recent)
```

I check these to make sure they look reasonable with some figures.

```{r}
#| label: fig-summary-age-dist
#| fig-cap: Summary measures of age distribution of spouses, interpolated and non-interpolated data
#| layout-ncol: 1
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - Mean age of husbands
#|   - Mean age of wives
#|   - Spousal Age gap

temp <- prop_age_year_recent |>
  group_by(YEAR) |>
  summarize(mean_age_husband = sum(age_group_husband * prop),
            mean_age_wife = sum(age_group_wife * prop),
            age_diff = mean_age_husband - mean_age_wife) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(interpolated = YEAR %in% years_interp)

ggplot(temp, aes(x = YEAR, y = mean_age_husband))+
  geom_line()+
  geom_point(aes(color = interpolated))+
  labs(x = "year", y = "mean husband's age")+
  theme_bw()

ggplot(temp, aes(x = YEAR, y = mean_age_wife))+
  geom_line()+
  geom_point(aes(color = interpolated))+
  labs(x = "year", y = "mean wife's age")+
  theme_bw()

ggplot(temp, aes(x = YEAR, y = age_diff))+
  geom_line()+
  geom_point(aes(color = interpolated))+
  labs(x = "year", y = "mean husband's age - mean wife's age")+
  theme_bw()
```

# Sample restrictions

Before fitting age weights, I should apply whatever global sample restrictions I need to apply to the data. 

I remove any missing values on race of spouses as these are groups that I did not explicitly code.

```{r}
#| label: drop-race-na

census <- census |>
  filter(!is.na(race_husband) & !is.na(race_wife))

```

# Calulate age weights

Now that I have the joint distribution of age for recent marriages, I can compute the same proportions across all extant marriages and then use the ratio of the proportions to get the weights, the same as for post-stratification weights.

```{r}
#| label: calculate-weights

prop_age_year <- census |>
  group_by(age_group_husband, age_group_wife, union_type, YEAR) |>
  summarize(n_dur = n()) |>
  ungroup()

prop_age_year <- census |>
  group_by(union_type, YEAR) |>
  summarize(n_total = n()) |>
  ungroup() |>
  right_join(prop_age_year, by = c("union_type", "YEAR")) |>
  mutate(prop_total = n_dur / n_total) |>
  select(age_group_husband, age_group_wife, union_type, YEAR, prop_total)

prop_age_year |>
  group_by(union_type, YEAR) |>
  summarize(sum = sum(prop_total)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = union_type, values_from = sum) |>
  gt()

weighting <- full_join(prop_age_year, prop_age_year_recent) |>
  mutate(weight_age = prop / prop_total,
         weight_age = ifelse(is.na(weight_age), 0, weight_age))

census <- census |>
  left_join(weighting)
```

I confirm that the mean of the weights in each year is 1.

```{r}
#| label: mean-weights

# confirm that the mean weight in each year is 1
census |>
  group_by(union_type, YEAR) |>
  summarize(mean = mean(weight_age)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = union_type, values_from = mean) |>
  gt()
```

As a test case, lets see how the weights adjust the distribution in 2008.

```{r}
#| label: fig-age-weights-hist
#| fig-cap: The distribution of husband's age in 2008. The dotted line gives the distribution of husband's age for recent marriages. The red histogram gives the distribution of husband's age across all observations, while the blue histogram applies age weights to the full distribution to bring them in line with recent marriages.

census |>
  filter(year == "2008" & union_type == "marriage") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age_husband, y = after_stat(density)))+
  geom_histogram(alpha = 0.7, fill = "red", binwidth = 1)+
  geom_histogram(alpha = 0.7, fill = "navy", binwidth = 1, 
                 aes(weight = weight_age))+
  geom_histogram(data = filter(census, year == "2008" & dur_mar <= 1),
               fill = NA, color = "black", linetype = 2, 
               binwidth = 1)+
  theme_bw()
```

# Save the data

Now lets save the data.

```{r}
#| label: save-analytical-data

# turn some variables into factors
census <- census |>
  mutate(year = factor(year),
         region = factor(region),
         division = factor(division),
         state = factor(state))

census <- census |> 
  rename(strata = STRATA, cluster = CLUSTER) |>
  select(union_type,
         race_husband, race_wife, 
         race_best_husband, race_best_wife,
         educ_husband, educ_wife, 
         age_husband, age_wife, 
         gen_husband, gen_wife,
         dur_mar,
         state, division, region, 
         weight_age, weight_sample, strata, cluster,
         year)
         

save(census, file = here("data", "data_constructed", "data_couples_married.RData"))
```
